Well, they're saying it's for VR which says at least something about the performance being reasonably high. They also use the words "starting at" a lot which gives me pause.

I agree though that there isn't enough information here to have a solid opinion about whether or not it's going to be as good as they claim. Caution is warranted. What I do find sorta funny is that HTC is saying "yes, this is what we need for better adoption!" and yet their VR equipment is arguably overpriced and a big part of what is hurting adoption.

Personally I'd argue that the Vive's pricepoint is ok considering you also get the motion controllers. I merely wish I could buy a Vive without them for a lower price, because I'm not interested in the room scale stuff all that much, even though I think it's cool. Similarly, VR without a computer capable of delivering stable 75+ FPS isn't going to cut it past showing how cool it is to your friends and family. VR equipment being overpriced or not, what's really hurting adoption is that it needs to stop being a gadget.

At the end of the day most normal people will not spend that much money on peripherals. If the objective is to raise adoption, HTC is doing it wrong because regular people can't justify spending that amount on something so limited in use. If HTC really wanted to push adoption, they'd get Valve to subsidise the hardware to bring the cost down to half of what it currently is. The long term win here is that Valve would make their money back in VR game sales as the flood of equipment to the market would spark a software gold rush to capitalise on. Think of it as similar to how Microsoft dominated the console market during the 360 era. Consoles were sold at a loss, and profit was made with the games.

We're not seeing a ton of developer interest right now because adoption hasn't been very good.
I'm interested in price/performance metric, but for that we need benchmarks. It can be a great card for $200 if it delivers 70% of GTX 1080 performance, which is somewhere around GTX 980 Ti.

Until the price of the headsets and any other equipment needed drops substantially, it's not going to be anything more than a cool thing for a niche group of technofiles. I'm looking forward to seeing the price drop to the point where mainstream adoption occurs and we start seeing massive amounts of new VR-based innovations.
